summary: Defines a data model, with an XML implementation, for intrusion detection alerts, so different intrusion detection systems and management tools can share information in a common format. This is an experimental RFC.

eli5.summary: Different burglar alarms speak different languages. IDMEF is a common form to fill in when an alarm goes off, so every system can read the same report.

subtitle: A common XML format that lets intrusion detection tools report alerts and heartbeats to the same consoles.

tldr.problem: Intrusion detection products each reported suspicious events in their own format, so mixing tools from different vendors, or feeding them to one database, correlator or console, was hard.
tldr.mechanism: IDMEF defines an object-oriented data model for alerts and heartbeats, then expresses it in XML with a DTD. An analyzer (sensor) sends these messages to a manager (console).
tldr.outcome: The RFC is Experimental and not a candidate for any level of Internet Standard. The IESG published it to document the work as it stood when the working group concluded and to encourage experimentation.

today: RFC 4765 is Experimental and, according to its IESG Note, is not a candidate for any level of Internet Standard. The unit metadata shows no RFC that obsoletes or updates it. Its companion requirements document is RFC 4766.

sections.title: Why a Common Alert Format
sections.content:
The Intrusion Detection Message Exchange Format (IDMEF) is meant to be a standard data format that automated intrusion detection systems use to report alerts about events they consider suspicious. The goal is interoperability among commercial, open source and research systems, so users can mix and match tools according to their strengths and weaknesses.

The obvious place to use it is the channel between an analyzer (also called a sensor) and the manager (also called a console) that receives its alarms. The RFC lists other uses too: a single database that stores results from many products, an event correlation system that accepts alerts from many products, a graphical interface that shows alerts from several products on one screen, and easier data exchange between users, vendors, response teams and law enforcement.

The IESG Note says the work was considered by the IETF but the working group concluded before it was approved as a standards-track protocol. The IETF disclaims any knowledge of the fitness of this RFC for any purpose, and readers are told to exercise caution in evaluating it for implementation and deployment.
sections.eli5: Imagine every shop in a mall had a different kind of alarm and a different kind of report form. IDMEF is one shared form, so the security office can read every report the same way.

sections.title: The Data Model and Its Design Goals
sections.content:
The IDMEF data model is an object-oriented representation of the alert data that analyzers send to managers. The RFC explains why that style fits: alerts carry very different amounts of information, analyzers get their data from network traffic, operating system logs or application audit trails, and vendors want to deliver more or less detail. Adding classes by aggregation or subclassing lets a receiver that does not know an extension still understand the subset defined by the model.

The model is content-driven: new objects are added to carry new content, not to express semantic differences between alerts. It must also be unambiguous. Analyzers may be more or less precise, but they must not contradict each other, so the information they have in common must be identical and sit in the same place. Putting interesting data in extension fields instead of its proper field reduces interoperability and should be avoided.

The model does not say how an alert should be classified. One analyzer may call a port scan a single attack on many targets, another may call it many attacks from one source. Once an analyzer has chosen what to send, the model dictates the format. Complex alerts that aggregate simple ones must be able to identify those simple alerts.

Two implementations were originally proposed to the Intrusion Detection Working Group (IDWG): an SNMP MIB and an XML DTD. At its February 2000 meeting the group decided the XML solution best fulfilled its requirements. The RFC gives XML's tooling, built-in support for UTF-8 and UTF-16 and per-element language marking, and its fit with filtering and aggregation, as reasons.
sections.eli5: The model is like a set of labelled boxes: one for who did it, one for what was hit, one for when. Everybody uses the same boxes, and you can add new boxes without breaking the old ones.

sections.title: Alerts and Heartbeats
sections.content:
Every IDMEF message is an IDMEF-Message, whose only attribute is version; applications that set it MUST use 1.0. There are two kinds of message: Alert and Heartbeat.

An Alert is sent whenever an analyzer detects an event it was configured to look for. It may cover one event or several, and alerts occur asynchronously. It must contain exactly one Analyzer, one CreateTime (the only required time) and one Classification. It may also carry DetectTime, AnalyzerTime, any number of Source and Target elements, an Assessment, and any number of AdditionalData elements. The optional messageid attribute identifies the alert.

An alert can additionally be one of three subclasses. A ToolAlert groups earlier alerts as the result of one attack tool or malicious program. A CorrelationAlert groups earlier alerts that are related. An OverflowAlert gives details of a buffer overflow attack: the program the attack tried to run (not the program attacked), plus optionally the size in bytes and some or all of the overflow data. Tool and correlation alerts list the related alerts with alertident elements, and an optional analyzerid says which analyzer sent each one.

A Heartbeat tells a manager that an analyzer is up. It is meant to be sent regularly, for example every ten minutes or every hour, and a missing run of heartbeats suggests the analyzer or its network connection has failed. Managers MUST support receiving heartbeats, but analyzers are free to skip them. A heartbeat holds an Analyzer, a CreateTime, and optionally a HeartbeatInterval in seconds, an AnalyzerTime and AdditionalData.
sections.eli5: An alert is a person shouting "something is wrong over there!". A heartbeat is the same person calling "all fine here" every so often, so you know they have not fallen asleep.

sections.title: Who, What and How Bad: the Core Classes
sections.content:
The Analyzer class says which tool produced the message. It has an analyzerid plus optional descriptive attributes such as name, manufacturer, model, version, ostype and osversion. Only the originating analyzer may be named, but a manager that forwards an alert may nest the original analyzer inside its own to allow analyzer path tracking.

Classification carries the alert's name chosen by the alert provider, in a required text attribute, and may point to outside documentation through Reference elements. A reference has an origin such as cve, bugtraqid, osvdb, vendor-specific or user-specific, a name and a url.

Source and Target describe where the events came from and where they were aimed. Each can hold a Node (host or device, with addresses), a User, a Process and a Service; a Target may also list File elements. Several of each are allowed, for example the many sources of a distributed denial of service. A source can be marked spoofed and a target decoy, with the values unknown (default), yes or no.

Assessment holds the analyzer's own judgement. Impact has a severity (info, low, medium, high), a completion (failed or succeeded) and a broad type. Action records what the analyzer did, such as block-installed, notification-sent or taken-offline. Confidence is either a rough low, medium or high, or a numeric posterior probability between 0.0 and 1.0. The RFC warns that confidence values from different analyzers should not be compared without care.

The support classes fill in the detail. A Service must give a name or a port, or a port list, and has WebService and SNMPService subclasses. A File can carry times, sizes, access permissions, links, Unix inode data and Checksum values. A UserId has a type such as current-user, original-user or target-user, so a privilege change can be shown.
sections.eli5: An alert answers the questions a detective asks: who is reporting, who did it, who or what was hit, what kind of trouble it was, and how sure and how worried we are.

sections.title: XML Rules and Data Types
sections.content:
IDMEF documents exchanged between compliant applications MUST begin with an XML declaration that gives the XML version, and naming the encoding is RECOMMENDED. Messages SHOULD NOT use encodings other than UTF-8 and UTF-16; with no encoding given, UTF-8 is assumed. A UTF-16 document MUST start with a byte order mark. Applications MUST say which language their content is in, usually with xml:lang on the top element, and all elements MUST support xml:space. The IDMEF namespace is http://iana.org/idmef.

Because XML is text, every value is written as text, and the RFC defines how each data type looks:

  • INTEGER: base 10 with an optional sign, or base 16 with a 0x prefix.
  • REAL: the POSIX strtod form; both . and , MUST be accepted as the radix character.
  • BYTE: binary data, which MUST be base64 encoded.
  • DATETIME: a subset of ISO 8601, for example YYYY-MM-DDThh:mm:ssZ, which MUST include either Z for UTC or an offset such as -05:00. Leap seconds MUST be supported.
  • NTPSTAMP: a 64-bit NTP timestamp written as two 32-bit hexadecimal values separated by a period, such as 0x12345678.0x87654321.
  • PORTLIST: comma-separated ports and ranges, such as 5-25,37,42,43,53,69-119,123-514.

Time elements carry both forms. The CreateTime, DetectTime and AnalyzerTime elements hold a date-time as content and a required ntpstamp attribute. If the two ever disagree, the NTP timestamp MUST be used.

Identifiers come in two kinds. An analyzerid must be unique across the analyzers in one intrusion detection environment, not globally, and an alert or heartbeat is identified by the pair (analyzerid, messageid). The ident attributes on classes such as Source, Target, Node and Service must be unique among the messages sent by one analyzer. Both default to 0, meaning the analyzer cannot generate unique identifiers. How to create the values is out of scope.
sections.eli5: Everything is written as plain text in a strict style, like filling in a form where the date, the number and the list of doors each have an exact way to be written.

sections.title: Extending IDMEF
sections.content:
The data model can be extended by inheritance (a subclass adds attributes) or aggregation (a whole gains parts). Inheritance is preferred because it preserves the existing structure and the operations on it.

For the XML form there are two routes, and both go through the AdditionalData class. For small items such as an integer or a string, AdditionalData with a type like integer, real, string or date-time and a free-text meaning attribute SHOULD be used whenever possible. For complex data, an extension DTD can be added as a module, with these MUST rules: the document declares the extension's namespace and DTD location, the extension declares all its elements and attributes in its own namespace and never in the idmef or default namespace, and the extension content appears only under an AdditionalData whose type is xml.

Receivers must be forgiving. An application MUST keep processing a well-formed message that contains tags it does not understand, and decides for itself what to do with that content. IDMEF documents MUST be well-formed and SHOULD be valid when that is possible and practical.
sections.eli5: If you need a new kind of note, you stick it in the "extra stuff" pocket with its own label. Anyone who does not understand it can ignore it and keep reading the rest.

sections.title: Clocks, Time Wrap-Around and Signatures
sections.content:
Synchronizing analyzer and manager clocks is outside the scope of the RFC, but it advises that all of them should use an external source such as NTP or SNTP whenever possible. When that is not possible, the AnalyzerTime element supports rudimentary synchronization. The sender puts its current clock value in AnalyzerTime as late as possible, ideally right before the message goes on the wire. The receiving manager computes the difference from its own clock and uses it to adjust CreateTime and DetectTime, including the NTP timestamps. Applications SHOULD let users turn this method on or off.

Relays complicate this. If intermediaries forward messages without adding delay, synchronization is end to end. If they may inject delay, synchronization MUST happen at each hop, which means unpacking the message, adjusting every time value and rebuilding it. In mixed environments every manager and intermediary must use AnalyzerTime synchronization.

NTP timestamps overflow in 2036. Applications MUST NOT send a zero timestamp unless they mean it to be invalid or unavailable. After 2036-02-07T06:28:16Z, compliant applications MUST follow the convention quoted from RFC 4330: if bit 0 is set, time counts from 1 January 1900; if not, it counts from 6h 28m 16s UTC on 7 February 2036.

The RFC leaves message integrity and authentication to the transport protocol, but where messages travel over less secure protocols or signatures must be archived, it RECOMMENDS the XML Signature standard. Details are out of scope.
sections.eli5: Two clocks in two rooms may not agree. The sender writes its own clock time on the note, and the receiver works out how far off it is and corrects the times.

sections.title: Worked Examples
sections.content:
The RFC gives complete messages for common situations, and says they are illustrations, not guidance on how alerts should be classified. They include the teardrop and ping of death denial-of-service attacks (the second shows several targets and a spoofed source), a port scan, a connection to a disallowed service, local attacks such as loadmodule and phf, file modification, a system policy violation, a correlated alert, an analyzer assessment, a heartbeat and an XML extension.

The correlated alert example restates a port scan as if a correlation engine had detected it. It adds a CorrelationAlert named multiple ports in short time, whose alertident elements list the underlying alerts, some from another analyzer. The assessment example is a host-based report of unauthorized root access through a buffer overflow. It records an Impact of high severity that succeeded with type admin, three actions (a page sent, a user disabled, a user logged out) and a Confidence rating of high.

The heartbeat example uses AdditionalData elements with meaning attributes to report the percentage of memory and disk used. The extension example shows a vendor adding geographic data (latitude, longitude and optional elevation) to a node by placing it under AdditionalData with type xml and tying it to the node through a matching identifier.
sections.eli5: The examples are sample filled-in forms, like a form for a break-in at the front door and another for a sensor saying it is still awake.

sections.title: Security Considerations
sections.content:
The RFC says there are no security concerns directly tied to the format of the data, but the data itself may be security-sensitive, so its confidentiality, integrity and availability may need protection. Systems that collect, send, process and store it should be protected against unauthorized use, and the data against unauthorized access. How to do that is outside the document.

The companion requirements document, RFC 4766, describes the security characteristics the transport protocol should have: message confidentiality, message integrity, non-repudiation and avoidance of duplicate messages. When a protocol without these properties carries IDMEF, digital signatures inside the message may help certify integrity.
sections.eli5: An alarm report can itself be a secret, like a map of where your locks are weak. So the way it travels and where it is kept must be protected too.

sections.title: IANA Registry and Future Changes
sections.content:
Many attributes take values from fixed lists. To let those lists grow, IANA created a repository called Intrusion Detection Message Exchange Format (IDMEF) Attribute Values. Its policy is Specification Required by RFC: a new value needs an RFC that includes the registration template, describes interoperability and security issues, and IANA assigns the next rank number in sequence. The RFC lists the initial values for every enumerated attribute.

Adding whole new classes or attributes is held to a higher bar. It requires IETF Consensus, meaning an RFC approved by the IESG. Such additions are for generally useful data that the current classes cannot represent cleanly; vendor-specific or obscure information is called a poor reason. The RFC anticipated that host-based intrusion detection would be the first area needing new classes, but only after some consensus on the data.
sections.eli5: There is an official list of allowed words. To add a word you have to write it up properly and get it approved, so everyone keeps using the same words.

data.title: Heartbeat message
data.code:
<?xml version="1.0" encoding="UTF-8"?>

<idmef:IDMEF-Message version="1.0"
               xmlns:idmef="http://iana.org/idmef">
  <idmef:Heartbeat messageid="abc123456789">
    <idmef:Analyzer analyzerid="hq-dmz-analyzer01">
      <idmef:Node category="dns">
        <idmef:name>analyzer01.example.com</idmef:name>
      </idmef:Node>
    </idmef:Analyzer>
    <idmef:CreateTime ntpstamp="0xbc722ebe.0x00000000">
      2000-03-09T14:07:58Z
    </idmef:CreateTime>
    <idmef:AdditionalData type="real" meaning="%memused">
      <idmef:real>62.5</idmef:real>
    </idmef:AdditionalData>
  </idmef:Heartbeat>
</idmef:IDMEF-Message>
